items.title: Sparse Matrix Multiplication Exponent 1.5 in the Low-bandwidth Model
items.summary: We study sparse matrix multiplication in the low-bandwidth model: $n$ computers multiply two $n\times n$ matrices, and each computer can send and receive one $O(\log n)$-bit message per round. The input matrices are uniformly sparse, meaning that there are at most $d$ nonzero entries in each row and column, and the task is to compute a uniformly sparse part of their product. In prior work, Gupta et al.~(SPAA 2022) presented an $O(d^{1.907})$-round algorithm over fields for this problem when the sparsity structure is globally known in advance (this is referred to as the supported setting). The upper bound was later improved to $O(d^{1.832})$ rounds. In this work, we give a deterministic algorithm that solves this problem in $O(d^{3/2})$ rounds in the supported setting, improving the previous bounds over fields and semirings.

items.title: Neural Render Proxies for Interactive and Differentiable Lighting
items.summary: Within the CG animation production pipeline, the challenges artists tackle in Lighting can be immense. Even minor adjustments require re-rendering massive scenes with slow offline renderers; global illumination has to be sampled and complex shaders have to be evaluated, leading to iteration times of minutes to hours per frame. To accelerate this process, we introduce a novel neural render proxy (NRP) that enables differentiable relighting of static scenes with fixed camera and materials at interactive rates. Our main insight is the decoupling of traditional rendering into path sampling and emission computation. From a single, light-agnostic render pass, we collect light transport data in the form of path samples. This enables rapidly sampling lighting conditions on the fly, and training a scene-specific lightweight neural network that learns how light is transported from any scene location to any image pixel. This approach is compatible with non-differentiable production renderers, induces minimal memory requirements during inference, and scales only with resolution and the number of light sources and parameters, but independently of scene and appearance complexity. Our evaluation demonstrates interactive frame rates for relighting (~30-60 Hz) while closely approximating the visual fidelity of ground-truth path tracing. In addition, the differentiable NRP enables fast, gradient-based inverse workflows, allowing artists to efficiently solve for lighting parameters from intuitive image-space edits or generative targets.

items.title: Internalizing Investment Mandates: A Neurosymbolic RL Approach to Portfolio Allocation
items.summary: Institutional portfolios operate under investment policy statements that specify asset allocation constraints, often conditioned on market regime information. Deep reinforcement learning has been shown to optimize financial performance but typically does not enforce rule compliance, making it unsuitable for real-world deployment. Existing neurosymbolic methods such as Probabilistic Logic Policy Gradient (PLPG) offer constraint-satisfying reinforcement learning (RL) via differentiable symbolic supervision but assume a finite, discrete action space. We present a PLPG-inspired continuous allocation method that estimates the probability that the policy's own executed action satisfies the investment mandate, using reparameterized Monte Carlo sampling, and adds it to the training objective. No post-hoc enforcement mechanism intercepts actions at inference time and compliance is learned by the agent. Audited directly on deterministic mean actions with no correction, the policy reduces violations of a six-rule regime-conditional mandate from 96-98% for unconstrained RL and 33.4% for a reward-penalty baseline to 4.8%, showing that a continuous-action neurosymbolic policy can substantially internalize a symbolic mandate.

items.title: Using an energy pixels approach to estimate the size a 2nd Generation DEL must be to train a high-resolution binding model
items.summary: DNA-encoded libraries (DELs) are commonly used to find small-molecule binders to a target protein. But the hard part is no longer finding a hit. It is building a machine-learning model good enough to guide the medicinal chemistry that follows, one that can resolve the shift in affinity when a chemist changes a single atom. Such a model needs two things from its training data: dense sampling of the small patch of chemical space around the hit, and an adequate number of genuinely tight binders within it. A diverse naive DEL gives neither. It samples an enormous space, so any one neighborhood is covered far too thinly, and the tightest binders are rare. A model trained on that naive DEL data must extrapolate to binders tighter than any it has seen, and that is where models can fail. One way to get training data with both properties is a second-generation DEL built around the hit. We ask how complex that library must be. We treat binding as a sum of small, independent interactions, called pixels on the target and antipixels on the ligand. From the spread of affinities measured in the naive library, with no structural information and nothing yet synthesized, we estimate the complexity such a library must have to supply that dense sampling and those tight binders. The method does two useful things. It turns the number of tight binders a model needs into the number of compounds a library must contain. And it estimates the expected yield of a randomly designed second-generation DEL, so the gain from designing the library with machine learning or active learning can be measured against a baseline, without the expense of a control library as large as the experiment itself.

items.title: Experience-Handoff Reinforcement Learning for Recursive Self-Improvement
items.summary: It is common to train Large Language Models (LLMs) for agentic tasks with Reinforcement Learning (RL) from scalar rewards. However, this throws away the fine-grained information about the environment that the agent experienced during the trial (e.g., error logs). To utilize this rich information, recent works wrap the agent in a harness that refines its own inputs through reflection or compaction and hands past experience to future rollouts, but the construction of the handed-off artifacts (e.g., a playbook) is itself not learned. We want the best of both worlds: gradient updates from a scalar reward, while also utilizing environment information to hand off experience. As a concrete testbed, we fix the Agentic Context Engineering () harness and train one model to act, reflect, and curate task-local playbooks. Our method, , evaluates candidate experience-handoff artifacts by their downstream effect on future actor rollouts, and co-optimizes the role-specific behaviors (action generator, insight reflector, and playbook curator) under a fixed scaffold. Across agentic benchmarks, achieves higher held-out performance than baseline methods. The results suggest that agent training should optimize not only the actions in the current rollout, but also the model-written experience that future rollouts inherit.

items.title: Vector-Space Projection and Unified Complex-Valued Acceleration for Scaling Matrix-Based Brain-Inspired Representations
items.summary: Symbolic reasoning at scale requires representations that are both expressive and hardware-efficient. Hyperdimensional Computing (HDC) provides a promising brain-inspired framework, encoding concepts as high-dimensional vectors composed through efficient algebraic operations. However, the widely used Fourier Holographic Reduced Representation (FHRR) relies on commutative binding, which cannot encode order or directionality. Prior FPGA/ASIC accelerators recover this through costly permutation logic, incurring irregular memory access and high control overhead. Generalized Holographic Reduced Representations (GHRR) instead redefine binding as non-commutative matrix multiplication, naturally encoding sequences, graphs, and hierarchies without permutations-but at the cost of turning every element into a matrix, introducing compute and storage overhead that limits scalability. In this work, we propose a flattening methodology that preserves GHRR's matrix-based encoding while executing training and inference directly in vector space, functionally equivalent to FHRR inference yet free of permutation logic. We further design a custom 28 nm ASIC that fuses binding and similarity into a unified complex-valued datapath, with dual-DMA streaming and runtime normalization for accurate inference. Against a PyTorch baseline on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU, the prototype delivers 1.36x-1.56x higher throughput and 16.2x-18.6x better energy efficiency.

items.title: An Agentic Python Framework for LLM-Driven UVM Testbench Synthesis with Closed-Loop Compiler Feedback

items.title: AMARA: Compiler-Driven Accelerator Architecture Design for Graphical Probabilistic Sampling
items.summary: Sampling methods are fundamental primitives for training and inference on probabilistic models. However, practical deployment of sampling algorithms such as Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) remains difficult on general-purpose processors. Existing hardware accelerators improve sampling efficiency, but they are typically specialized for a narrow class of models, graph topologies, or update schedules, making it difficult to support the diverse workloads used in real applications. This paper presents AMARA, an end-to-end compiler-driven accelerator framework for probabilistic sampling on arbitrary probabilistic graphical models. AMARA introduces MCMC-IR, a domain-specific intermediate representation that separates local factorized computation from global update dependencies. Based on this representation, the compiler performs architecture-aware partitioning, scheduling, and memory-access optimization to expose parallelism and reduce irregular graph communication. The optimized program is lowered to a compact ISA and executed on a programmable ASIC accelerator with specialized compute, sampling, and memory support. By co-designing the compiler and the architecture, AMARA bridges the gap between model generality and accelerator efficiency for practical MCMC-based probabilistic computing. We evaluate AMARA across representative workloads with different structures, including grid-structured and irregular energy-based models, and causal inference networks. The results show that AMARA supports a broad spectrum of discrete probabilistic models while achieving high sampling throughput and efficient hardware utilization. AMARA achieves an average of 6.1$\times$ (up to 16.3$\times$) higher sampling throughput than a JAX-GPU baseline on irregular workloads, and offers broader programmability than state-of-the-art accelerators.

items.title: Recompute or Restore? Host-Tier KV for Multi-Model Agent Workflows on a Static-Graph NPU Serving Stack
items.summary: Agent workflows issue dependent model calls that share long context prefixes, so serving them efficiently depends on reusing the key-value (KV) cache of those prefixes. On accelerators that compile model graphs ahead of time, however, the device KV budget is fixed, and prefixes evicted under load must be recomputed. Restoring them from host memory avoids this recomputation, but the transfer occupies the same engine thread as prefill and decode, so its benefit is not guaranteed. In this paper, we study when restoring beats recomputing on a commercial static-graph neural processing unit (NPU) stack (Rebellions ATOM+, vllm-rbln 0.10.2) that serves a Qwen3-8B planner on two cards and a Qwen3-0.6B executor on one. We first show that repeated prefill dominates planner work when default serving collapses: 89.5% of the executed planner prompt tokens had been materialized before. We then build a synchronous host-DRAM tier on the runtime's public KV copy calls, together with a scheduler-aware event model whose predictions are frozen before each test cohort. Experimental results show that the host tier raises workflow service-level objective (SLO) attainment from 22.8% to 100% and from 9.4% to 99.8% in the two tested overload conditions, and endpoint confirmation on two new seeds supports conservative load gains of 11.8% (chain) and 18.2% (fork), while mixed and bursty workloads remain seed-sensitive. The frozen model predicts median and 99th-percentile (P99) latency within its 15% tolerance in all 24 common-load conditions, including the 16-18% P99 increase that the tier causes for fork workflows, but it misorders three policy contrasts and overestimates the benefit of a cheaper store path (11% predicted against 3.1% measured). The trade-off therefore depends on runtime scheduling and transfer cost as well as cache capacity.

items.title: From Delegation to Coordination: Learning Efficient Multi-Agent Deep Research
items.summary: Multi-agent deep-research systems use delegation to parallelize search and keep long tool traces out of the main agent's context. Yet delegation helps only when task allocation and subtask execution are coordinated: the main agent must issue useful subtasks, while subagents must return reliable evidence. Existing training either optimizes only the main agent or broadcasts the same team advantage to all agents, which can reward misleading subagent reports and penalize useful ones. We introduce LEAD-RL (Learning Effective Agent Delegation with Reinforcement Learning), a joint main-agent-subagent training framework with contribution-aware credit assignment. A training-time rubric evaluates the research utility of each subagent report and gates its inherited team advantage, while final-answer correctness remains the only team reward; no token, step, or speedup reward is used. Across five benchmarks and two model families, LEAD-RL improves answer quality. On BrowseComp, it improves accuracy by 2.49 percentage points and reduces critical-path cost by 24.5% over joint training with shared team credit. During validation, accuracy increases by 6.78 points at approximately constant critical-path cost. These results show that contribution-aware credit assignment improves the quality-efficiency trade-off of multi-agent deep research.

items.title: SPEC CPU2026 Under the Microscope: Programs, Phases, and Samples
items.summary: SPEC CPU2026, the latest generation of the SPEC CPU benchmarks, is set to become the standard benchmark suite in computer architecture research, where new designs are often evaluated through sampled simulation with tools such as SimPoint. Existing characterizations of the suite focus on whole-run averages, which reveal neither how behavior changes within a run nor how well sampling captures it. We characterize CPU2026 on real hardware at three levels: programs, phases, and samples. At the program level, we report whole-run metrics and top-down bottleneck classes for all four suites and examine how they change with workload size, compiler version, and platform, across machines with three different instruction set architectures: x86, Arm, and RISC-V. Notably, changing only the compiler version can halve or nearly double the IPC of individual benchmarks. At the phase level, we track hardware counters every 10 ms over all 90 SPECrate inputs, identify recurring patterns of time-varying behavior, and divide the inputs into three groups: steady, multi-phase, and bursty. More than half of the inputs show time-varying behavior, and IPC within a single input can vary by more than an order of magnitude. At the sample level, we validate SimPoint against hardware measurements of every interval it can select. SimPoint is accurate on steady inputs, but its error reaches 43% on the others, and changing only the random seed spreads the error of one input over a range of 58 percentage points. Keeping SimPoint's clusters but choosing each representative by measured CPI brings every input within 2.6%, so the error comes from the choice of representatives, not from the clustering. We conclude with practical recommendations on sampling strategy for CPU2026, which give researchers a deeper understanding of the suite and show where additional simulation effort is needed to keep sampled results accurate.

items.title: Collaborative Task Allocation for Heterogeneous Multi-Robot Systems Through Iterative Clustering
items.summary: Multi-robot systems face the challenge of efficiently allocating teams of heterogeneous robots to tasks. The task allocation problem is complicated by collaborative interactions between robots where teams of robots develop emergent capabilities that enable them to complete tasks that would be inefficient or impossible for individual robots. To address these challenges, we present an iterative clustering algorithm for collaborative task allocation in heterogeneous multi-robot systems. This approach partitions the computationally intractable global optimization problem into smaller, tractable subproblems by iteratively forming clusters of robots and tasks, then optimizing assignments within each cluster. By ensuring robots remain clustered with their currently assigned tasks, we guarantee monotonic improvement in overall utility with each iteration. We analyze the convergence of the algorithm and characterize how cluster size constraints determine which suboptimal assignments could trap the algorithm. In simulation, iterative clustering consistently outperforms simulated annealing, and a group-based auction in both computation time and solution quality, and outperforms a hedonic game approach in solution quality.

items.title: FIRE: Failure Isolation and Reliability for Production-Connected Experiments at Scale
items.summary: Pre-production changes are usually tested in isolated environments to prevent their side effects from reaching production. Some record-and-replay platforms allow a production-connected mode: candidate changes receive recorded production requests while selected downstream calls reach production dependencies. This improves fidelity before deployment, but it also introduces reliability risks. At hyperscale, experimental traffic can fan out across shared services, trigger latent defects, or send malformed input to systems serving user requests. In this paper, we show how production-connected experimentation can operate reliably in a large-scale recommendation serving system. To contain downstream effects without sacrificing realistic dependency behavior, the platform uses three complementary guardrails. Isolated tiers redirect replay traffic away from shared dependencies where replication is practical. Dependency monitors observe downstream health and experiment-attributed errors and terminate experiments after sustained violations. Traffic pinning limits experimental calls to a designated subset of downstream workers when full replication would require scarce capacity. Isolated ranking tiers process billions of replayed requests per day using under 1% of the corresponding serving capacity. Over 90 days, these tiers experienced more than 200,000 abnormal worker exits without directly affecting production-serving workers. During a separate three-month window, dependency monitors cancelled approximately 5% of experiments for the measured ranking service and accounted for 87% of its cancellations. Dependency-aware triggering also reduced code-review experiment executions by 25%. These results show that high-fidelity, production-connected experimentation can operate at scale when downstream effects are isolated where possible, bounded where necessary, and continuously monitored and attributed.

items.title: Gradient-based Planning for World Models at Longer Horizons
items.summary:
GRASP is a new gradient-based planner for learned dynamics (a "world model") that makes long-horizon planning practical by (1) lifting the trajectory into virtual states so optimization is parallel across time, (2) adding stochasticity directly to the state iterates for exploration, and (3) reshaping gradients so actions get clean signals while we avoid brittle "state-input" gradients through high-dimensional vision models. Large, learned world models are becoming increasingly capable. They can predict long sequences of future observations in high-dimensional visual spaces and generalize across tasks in ways that were difficult to imagine a few years ago. As these models scale, they start to look less like task-specific predictors and more like general-purpose simulators. But having a powerful predictive model is not the same as being able to use it effectively for control/learning/planning. In practice, long-horizon planning with modern world models remains fragile: optimization becomes ill-conditioned, non-greedy structure creates bad local minima, and high-dimensional latent spaces introduce subtle failure modes. In this blog post, I describe the problems that motivated this project and our approach to address them: why planning with modern world models can be surprisingly fragile, why long horizons are the real stress test, and what we changed to make gradient-based planning much more robust. This blog post discusses work done with Mike Rabbat, Aditi Krishnapriyan, Yann LeCun, and Amir Bar (* denotes equal advisorship), where we propose GRASP. What is a world model? These days, the term "world model" is quite overloaded, and depending on the context can either mean an explicit dynamics model or some implicit, reliable internal state that a generative model relies on (e.g. when an LLM generates chess moves, whether there is some internal representation of the board). We give our loose working definition below. Suppose you take actions $a_t \in \mathcal{A}$ and observe states $s_t \in \mathcal{S}$ (images, latent vectors, proprioception). A world model is a learned model that, given the current state and a sequence of future actions, predicts what will happen next. Formally, it defines a predictive distribution on a sequence of observed states $s_{t-h:t}$ and current action $a_t$: \[P_	heta(s_{t+1} \mid s_{t-h:t},\; a_t)\] that approximates the environment's true conditional $P(s_{t+1} \mid s_{t-h:t},\; a_t)$. For this blog post, we'll assume a Markovian model $P(s_{t+1} \mid s_{t-h:t},\; a_t)$ for simplicity (all results here can be extended to the more general case), and when the model is deterministic it reduces to a map over states: \[s_{t+1} = F_	heta(s_t, a_t).\] In practice the state $s_t$ is often a learned latent representation (e.g., encoded from pixels), so the model operates in a (theoretically) compact, differentiable space. The key point is that a world model gives you a differentiable simulator ; you can roll it forward under hypothetical action sequences and backpropagate through the predictions. Planning: choosing actions by optimizing through the model Given a start $s_0$ and a goal $g$, the simplest planner chooses an action sequence $\mathbf{a}=(a_0,\dots,a_{T-1})$ by rolling out the model and minimizing terminal error: \[\min_{\mathbf{a}} \; \| s_T(\mathbf{a}) - g \|_2^2, \quad 	ext{where } s_T(\mathbf{a}) = \mathcal{F}_{	heta}^{T}(s_0,\mathbf{a}).\] Here we use $\mathcal{F}^T$ as shorthand for the full rollout through the world model (dependence on model parameters $	heta$ is implicit): \[\mathcal{F}_{	heta}^{T}(s_0, \mathbf{a}) = F_	heta(F_	heta(\cdots F_	heta(s_0, a_0), \cdots, a_{T-2}), a_{T-1}).\] In short horizons and low-dimensional systems, this can work reasonably well. But as horizons grow and models become larger and more expressive, its weaknesses become amplified. So why doesn't this just work at scale? Why long-horizon planning is hard (even when everything is differentiable) There are two separate pain points for the more general world model, plus a third that is specific to learned, deep learning-based models. 1) Long-horizon rollouts create deep, ill-conditioned computation graphs Those familiar with backprop through time (BPTT) may notice that we're differentiating through a model applied to itself repeatedly, which will lead to the exploding/vanishing gradients problem. Namely, if we take derivatives (note we're differentiating vector-valued functions, resulting in Jacobians that we denote with $D_x (\cdots)$) with respect to earlier actions (e.g. $a_0$): \[D_{a_0} \mathcal{F}_{	heta}^{T}(s_0, \mathbf{a}) = \Bigl(\prod_{t=1}^T D_s F_	heta(s_t, a_t)\Bigr) D_{a_0}F_	heta(s_0, a_0).\] We see that the Jacobian's conditioning scales exponentially with time $T$: \[\sigma_{	ext{max/min}}(D_{a_0}\mathcal{F}_{	heta}^{T}) \sim \sigma_{	ext{max/min}}(D_s F_	heta)^{T-1},\] leading to exploding or vanishing gradients. 2) The landscape is non-greedy and full of traps At short horizons, the greedy solution, where we move straight toward the goal at every step, is often good enough. If you only need to plan a few steps ahead, the optimal trajectory usually doesn't deviate much from "head toward $g$" at each step. As horizons grow, two things happen. First, longer tasks are more likely to require non-greedy behavior: going around a wall, repositioning before pushing, backing up to take a better path. And as horizons grow, more of these non-greedy steps are typically needed. Second, the optimization space itself scales with horizon: $\mathrm{dim}(\mathcal{A} 	imes \cdots 	imes \mathcal{A}) = T\mathrm{dim}(\mathcal{A})$, further expanding the space of local minima for the optimization problem. Distance to goal along the optimal path is non-monotonic, and the resulting loss landscape can be rough. A long-horizon fix: lifting the dynamics constraint Suppose we treat the dynamics constraint $s_{t+1} = F_{	heta}(s_t, a_t)$ as a soft constraint, and we instead optimize the following penalty function over both actions $(a_0,\ldots,a_{T-1})$ and states $(s_0,\ldots,s_T)$: \[\min_{\mathbf{s},\mathbf{a}} \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{a}) = \sum_{t=0}^{T-1}  ig\|F_	heta(s_t,a_t) - s_{t+1} ig\|_2^2, \quad 	ext{with } s_0 	ext{ fixed and } s_T=g.\] This is also sometimes called collocation in planning/robotics literature. Note the lifted formulation shares the same global minimizers as the original rollout objective (both are zero exactly when the trajectory is dynamically feasible). But the optimization landscapes are very different, and we get two immediate benefits: Each world model evaluation $F_{	heta}(s_t,a_t)$ depends only on local variables, so all $T$ terms can be computed in parallel across time , resulting in a huge speed-up for longer horizons, and You no longer backpropagate through a single deep $T$-step composition to get a learning signal, since the previous product of Jacobians now splits into a sum, e.g.: \[D_{a_0} \mathcal{L} = 2(F_	heta(s_0, a_0) - s_1).\] Being able to optimize states directly also helps with exploration, as we can temporarily navigate through unphysical domains to find the optimal plan: Collocation-based planning allows us to directly perturb states and explore midpoints more effectively. However, lunch is never free. And indeed, especially for deep learning-based world models, there is a critical issue that makes the above optimization quite difficult in practice. An issue for deep learning-based world models: sensitivity of state-input gradients The tl;dr of this section is: directly optimizing states through a deep learning-based $F_{	heta}$ is incredibly brittle, à la adversarial robustness . Even if you train your world model in a lower-dimensional state space, the training process for the world model makes unseen state landscapes very sharp, whether it be an unseen state itself or simply a normal/orthogonal direction to the data manifold. Adversarial robustness and the "dimpled manifold" model Adversarial robustness originally looked at classification models $f_	heta : \mathbb{R}^{w	imes h 	imes c} 	o \mathbb{R}^K$, and showed that by following the gradient of a particular logit $
abla f_	heta^k$ from a base image $x$ (not of class $k$), you did not have to move far along $x' = x + \epsilon
abla f_	heta^k$ to make $f_	heta$ classify $x'$ as $k$ ( Szegedy et al., 2014 ; Goodfellow et al., 2015 ): Depiction of the classic example from (Goodfellow et al., 2015). Later work has painted a geometric picture for what's going on: for data near a low-dimensional manifold $\mathcal{M}$, the training process controls behavior in tangential directions, but does not regularize behavior in orthogonal directions, thus leading to sensitive behavior ( Stutz et al., 2019 ). Another way stated: $f_	heta$ has a reasonable Lipschitz constant when considering only tangential directions to the data manifold $\mathcal{M}$, but can have very high Lipschitz constants in normal directions. In fact, it often benefits the model to be sharper in these normal directions, so it can fit more complicated functions more precisely. As a result, such adversarial examples are incredibly common even for a single given model. Further, this is not just a computer vision phenomenon; adversarial examples also appear in LLMs ( Wallace et al., 2019 ) and in RL ( Gleave et al., 2019 ). While there are methods to train for more adversarially robust models, there is a known trade-off between model performance and adversarial robustness ( Tsipras et al., 2019 ): especially in the presence of many weakly-correlated variables, the model must be sharper to achieve higher performance. Indeed, most modern training algorithms, whether in computer vision or LLMs, do not train adversarial robustness out. Thus, at least until deep learning sees a major regime change, this is a problem we're stuck with . Why is adversarial robustness an issue for world model planning? Consider a single component of the dynamics loss we're optimizing in the lifted state approach: \[\min_{s_t, a_t, s_{t+1}} \|F_	heta(s_t, a_t) - s_{t+1}\|_2^2\] Let's further focus on just the base state: \[\min_{s_t} \|F_	heta(s_t, a_t) - s_{t+1}\|_2^2.\] Since world models are typically trained on state/action trajectories $(s_1, a_1, s_2, a_2, \ldots)$, the state-data manifold for $F_{	heta}$ has dimensionality bounded by the action space: \[\mathrm{dim}(\mathcal{M}_s) \le \mathrm{dim}(\mathcal{A}) + 1 + \mathrm{dim}(\mathcal{R}),\] where $\mathcal{R}$ is some optional space of augmentations (e.g. translations/rotations). Thus, we can typically expect $\mathrm{dim}(\mathcal{M}_s)$ to be much lower than $\mathrm{dim}(\mathcal{S})$, and thus: it is very easy to find adversarial examples that hack any state to any other desired state. As a result, the dynamics optimization \[\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}  ig\|F_	heta(s_t,a_t) - s_{t+1} ig\|_2^2\] feels incredibly "sticky," as the base points $s_t$ can easily trick $F_{	heta}$ into thinking it's already made its local goal. 1 1. This adversarial robustness issue, while particularly bad for lifted-state approaches, is not unique to them. Even for serial optimization methods that optimize through the full rollout map $\mathcal{F}^T$, it is possible to get into unseen states, where it is very easy to have a normal component fed into the sensitive normal components of $D_s F_{	heta}$. The action Jacobian's chain rule expansion is \[\Bigl(\prod_{t=1}^T D_s F_	heta(s_t, a_t)\Bigr) D_{a_0}F_	heta(s_0, a_0).\] See what happens if any stage of the product has any component normal to the data manifold. ↩ Our fix This is where our new planner GRASP comes in. The main observation: while $D_s F_{	heta}$ is untrustworthy and adversarial, the action space is usually low-dimensional and exhaustively trained, so $D_a F_{	heta}$ is actually reasonable to optimize through and doesn't suffer from the adversarial robustness issue! The action input is usually lower-dimensional and densely trained (the model has seen every action direction), so action gradients are much better behaved. At its core, GRASP builds a first-order lifted state / collocation-based planner that is only dependent on action Jacobians through the world model. We thus exploit the differentiability of learned world models $F_{	heta}$, while not falling victim to the inherent sensitivity of the state Jacobians $D_s F_{	heta}$. GRASP: Gradient RelAxed S tochastic P lanner As noted before, we start with the collocation planning objective, where we lift the states and relax dynamics into a penalty: \[\min_{\mathbf{s},\mathbf{a}} \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{a}) = \sum_{t=0}^{T-1}  ig\|F_	heta(s_t,a_t) - s_{t+1} ig\|_2^2, \quad 	ext{with } s_0 	ext{ fixed and } s_T=g.\] We then make two key additions. Ingredient 1: Exploration by noising the state iterates Even with a smoother objective, planning is nonconvex. We introduce exploration by injecting Gaussian noise into the virtual state updates during optimization. A simple version: \[s_t \leftarrow s_t - \eta_s 
abla_{s_t}\mathcal{L} + \sigma_{	ext{state}} \xi, \qquad \xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I).\] Actions are still updated by non-stochastic descent: \[a_t \leftarrow a_t - \eta_a 
abla_{a_t}\mathcal{L}.\] The state noise helps you "hop" between basins in the lifted space, while the actions remain guided by gradients. We found that specifically noising states here (as opposed to actions) finds a good balance of exploration and the ability to find sharper minima. 2 2. Because we only noise the states (and not the actions), the corresponding dynamics are not truly Langevin dynamics. ↩ Ingredient 2: Reshape gradients: stop brittle state-input gradients, keep action gradients As discussed, the fragile pathway is the gradient that flows into the state input of the world model, \(D_s F_{	heta}\) . The most straightforward way to do this initially is to just stop state gradients into \(F_{	heta}\) directly: Let $ ar{s}_t$ be the same value as $s_t$, but with gradients stopped. Define the stop-gradient dynamics loss : \[\mathcal{L}_{	ext{dyn}}^{	ext{sg}}(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{a}) = \sum_{t=0}^{T-1}  ig\|F_	heta( ar{s}_t, a_t) - s_{t+1} ig\|_2^2.\] This alone does not work. Notice now states only follow the previous state's step, without anything forcing the base states to chase the next ones. As a result, there are trivial minima for just stopping at the origin, then only for the final action trying to get to the goal in one step. Dense goal shaping We can view the above issue as the goal's signal being cut off entirely from previous states. One way to fix this is to simply add a dense goal term throughout prediction: \[\mathcal{L}_{	ext{goal}}^{	ext{sg}}(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{a}) = \sum_{t=0}^{T-1}  ig\|F_	heta( ar{s}_t, a_t) - g ig\|_2^2.\] In normal settings this would over-bias towards the greedy solution of straight chasing the goal, but this is balanced in our setting by the stop-gradient dynamics loss's bias towards feasible dynamics. The final objective is then as follows: \[\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{a}) = \mathcal{L}_{	ext{dyn}}^{	ext{sg}}(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{a}) + \gamma \, \mathcal{L}_{	ext{goal}}^{	ext{sg}}(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{a}).\] The result is a planning optimization objective that does not have dependence on state gradients. Periodic "sync": briefly return to true rollout gradients The lifted stop-gradient objective is great for fast, guided exploration , but it's still an approximation of the original serial rollout objective. So every $K_{	ext{sync}}$ iterations, GRASP does a short refinement phase: Roll out from $s_0$ using current actions $\mathbf{a}$, and take a few small gradient steps on the original serial loss: \[\mathbf{a} \leftarrow \mathbf{a} - \eta_{	ext{sync}}\,
abla_{\mathbf{a}}\,\|s_T(\mathbf{a})-g\|_2^2.\] The lifted-state optimization still provides the core of the optimization, while this refinement step adds some assistance to keep states and actions grounded towards real trajectories. This refinement step can of course be replaced with a serial planner of your choice (e.g. CEM); the core idea is to still get some of the benefit of the full-path synchronization of serial planners, while still mostly using the benefits of the lifted-state planning. How GRASP addresses long-range planning Collocation-based planners offer a natural fix for long-horizon planning, but this optimization is quite difficult through modern world models due to adversarial robustness issues. GRASP proposes a simple solution for a smoother collocation-based planner, alongside stable stochasticity for exploration . As a result, longer-horizon planning ends up not only succeeding more, but also finding such successes faster: Push-T demo: longer-horizon planning with GRASP. Horizon CEM GD LatCo GRASP H=40 61.4% / 35.3s 51.0% / 18.0s 15.0% / 598.0s 59.0% / 8.5s H=50 30.2% / 96.2s 37.6% / 76.3s 4.2% / 1114.7s 43.4% / 15.2s H=60 7.2% / 83.1s 16.4% / 146.5s 2.0% / 231.5s 26.2% / 49.1s H=70 7.8% / 156.1s 12.0% / 103.1s 0.0% / — 16.0% / 79.9s H=80 2.8% / 132.2s 6.4% / 161.3s 0.0% / — 10.4% / 58.9s Push-T results. Success rate (%) / median time to success. Bold = best in row. Note the median success time will bias higher with higher success rate; GRASP manages to be faster despite higher success rate. What's next? There is still plenty of work to be done for modern world model planners. We want to exploit the gradient structure of learned world models, and collocation (lifted-state optimization) is a natural approach for long-horizon planning, but it's crucial to understand typical gradient structure here: smooth and informative action gradients and brittle state gradients. We view GRASP as an initial iteration for such planners. Extension to diffusion-based world models (deeper latent timesteps can be viewed as smoothed versions of the world model itself), more sophisticated optimizers and noising strategies, and integrating GRASP into either a closed-loop system or RL policy learning for adaptive long-horizon planning are all natural and interesting next steps. I do genuinely think it's an exciting time to be working on world model planners. It's a funny sweet spot where the background literature (planning and control overall) is incredibly mature and well-developed, but the current setting (pure planning optimization over modern, large-scale world models) is still heavily underexplored. But, once we figure out all the right ideas, world model planners will likely become as commonplace as RL. For more details, read the full paper or visit the project website . items.title: CT-SGAL-LIO: Causal Continuous Time Refinement of Discrete LiDAR Inertial Odometry
items.summary: State-of-the-art LiDAR-inertial odometry methods, including those on richer state manifolds, achieve strong global accuracy, yet their pose stream alternates between propagation and correction and can oscillate over short horizons even when globally accurate. Most existing methods follow these approaches: they either modify the filter to enable faster updates or estimate a continuous-time trajectory from raw LiDAR and inertial data. The latter involves extra optimization, delaying state updates and becoming less robust during rapid rotations or accelerations. We propose CT-SGAL-LIO, a continuous-time refinement module that smooths the posterior pose stream of a discrete SGal(3) estimator without modifying the estimator itself. The key novelty is to perform continuous-time trajectory refinement directly on the projected SGal(3) posterior: we fit a cubic trajectory over a bounded window of recent poses and evaluate it at a small fixed lag. This places the query time within the observed interval, so the refined pose is obtained by interpolation rather than extrapolation, while preserving causal operation. CT-SGAL-LIO improves relative trajectory accuracy on 17 sequences from three public benchmarks. Across 17 sequences from GRAND-TOUR, MCD, and GEODE, CT-SGAL-LIO improves short-term motion accuracy while largely preserving global accuracy. RTE improves by up to 70% on GRAND-TOUR and on all seven GEODE sequences, with 9.9-51.1% reductions. A 19.5-min R-Campus run also reduces posterior jumps by 85.4% with only a 4.7 mm change in the end-to-start gap. We plan to release our source code and results to support community validation and reproducibility.

items.title: SALA: Semantically Aligned Latent Actions Enable Dual-Axis Scaling of Embodied Foundation Models
items.summary: Embodied foundation models hinge on diverse robot interaction data, which are costly to collect. Egocentric human videos offer a complementary source of experience, and latent action models (LAMs) provide a popular means of leveraging these videos for policy supervision. Compared with world-action models (WAMs), LAMs can offer greater training efficiency and potentially lower inference costs by avoiding explicit pixel prediction during policy learning and execution. However, most existing LAMs learn latent actions solely through video reconstruction, which can cause their representations to cluster by visual appearance rather than by the underlying actions. As a result, they struggle to align human actions with their robot counterparts. To bridge the gap, we introduce SALA, which emphasizes establishing the semantic correspondence for latent actions. Without requiring paired data, we use the language descriptions of unpaired human and robot clips to estimate semantic similarities and supervise cross-embodiment correspondence. Specifically, we translate these similarities into soft neighborhood structures that guide human latent actions toward semantically related robot latents, while robot action reconstruction grounds the latent space in control. The resulting shared latent action space provides a unified supervision signal for training an embodied foundation model on both human and robot videos. Notably, latent action supervision enables scaling along two axes: (1) pre-training on increasing amounts of general human video consistently reduces robot action prediction error on downstream tasks, and (2) post-training on increasing amounts of task-specific human video substantially improves real-world robot task success rates.

items.title: Machine Learning for Scalable Multi-AP Coordination in IEEE 802.11bn Networks
items.summary: As Wi-Fi deployments become denser, fully distributed random channel access no longer guarantees the required quality of service. The multi-access point coordination (MAPC) framework introduced in IEEE~802.11bn lets neighboring access points (APs) cooperate, but choosing which APs transmit together and how to configure them remains an open, computationally hard problem. We develop and validate a stack of machine learning (ML) coordination methods, progressing from lightweight hierarchical multi-armed bandits (H-MABs) to a generative pipeline built on graph neural networks (GNNs) and flow matching (FM). The methods are evaluated in simulation and on a hardware testbed, improving throughput over legacy access and scaling coordination to dozens of APs where analytical and search-based methods become intractable.

items.title: MegaOps: A Kernel Overlapping Framework with PyTorch-like Modularity and Megakernel Performance
items.summary: Modern ML frameworks execute models using the kernel-per-operator paradigm, which runs each operator as a separate GPU kernel. This paradigm is modular, since developers can compose various kernel implementations and profile each kernel in isolation. However, this paradigm enforces dependencies at the granularity of entire kernels, which places a barrier between dependent kernels. These barriers cause streaming multiprocessors to idle, serialize computation and communication, and prevent a kernel from prefetching its weights while the preceding kernel runs. Megakernels remove kernel barriers by fusing the operators of an entire layer or model into a single kernel, but they give up the modularity of the kernel-per-operator paradigm. In this work, we ask whether a kernel-per-operator ML framework can perform on par with megakernels. Our key insight is that removing kernel barriers does not require fusing kernels. We develop MegaOps, a framework that launches dependent kernels on separate CUDA streams and enforces each dependency on individual tiles of the intermediate tensor that the producer kernel writes and the consumer kernel reads. Since kernels synchronize on data tiles instead of on each other's thread blocks, any two kernels that adopt the same data tiling can be composed without modifying either kernel. We evaluate MegaOps on dense Llama3 and Qwen3 models on single H100, A100, and L40 GPUs and on multi-GPU servers with 4$\times$A100 and 8$\times$H100. Our MegaOps framework matches the throughput of hand-tuned ThunderKittens megakernels, and achieves 1.09$\times$-1.10$\times$ the decode throughput and 0.98$\times$-1.10$\times$ the prefill throughput of the best-performing baseline, while reusing existing Triton, cuBLAS, and cuDNN kernels.

items.title: Energy Aware Optimization of Non-Deterministic Task-Based Intermittent Computing Nodes with Thimble
items.summary: Intermittent computing nodes run on harvested energy, which they store in capacitors and spend in short bursts of computation. Choosing those capacitors is a trade-off: large capacitors can power large tasks but leak more current, wasting harvested energy, while small capacitors leak less but cannot power large tasks. Recent work, LEACS, showed that selecting capacitors and mapping tasks to them at compile time improves inference throughput. However, LEACS optimizes the mapping for a predetermined workload, whereas sensor nodes often run data-dependent workloads in which the next task depends on the outcome of earlier ones. We present Thimble, an energy storage system that maps a node's tasks to capacitors at runtime. Thimble models the workload as a Markov chain over tasks and assigns each task to a capacitor by weighing capacitor leakage, the task's energy demand and, when it replans, the likelihood of each future task. We compare Thimble against a reimplementation of LEACS, which ranks every static plan by simulation. When the training trace resembles deployment, Thimble's single design-time solve comes within 0.3--4% of LEACS's throughput. When the deployment conditions drift from the characteristics of the training set, LEACS's throughput-focused static plans can fail sharply. On the lowest-power source we consider, LEACS's plan stalls on deployment traces that harvest less than its training trace, and on some never wakes; Thimble avoids this, with 22--29% higher throughput at the reference workload. A sensitivity sweep over 25 workload profiles on that source shows that Thimble with depth replanning leads LEACS by 22--42% throughout, and what run-time remapping adds: replanning at a fixed interval matches or improves on the static map at 21 of 25 points, by up to 7%.

items.title: SubGPU Pipelining: Intra-GPU Fine-Grained Spatial Parallelism for LLM Inference
items.summary: Large language model (LLM) decode is dominated by short, predominantly memory-bound kernels that make bursty use of on-chip execution resources and memory bandwidth. This paper introduces SubGPU Pipelining, a fine-grained, intra-GPU spatial execution model that cuts an operator graph into ordered contiguous segments, binds those segments to spatial stages backed by disjoint streaming-multiprocessor (SM) pools, and streams microbatches through the resulting schedule. Selecting the graph cuts, segment-to-stage binding, per-stage SM allocation, and microbatch size is a coupled optimization problem: each choice changes the overlap pattern, shared-resource contention, cache state, and execution times of the others. We evaluate SubGPU Pipelining through both simulation and silicon experiment using the GPT-OSS 120B workload with 32-GPU B200 deployment settings. The analytical shared-resource simulator searches across SubGPU pipeline structures and batch sizes to map the per-user/per-GPU throughput Pareto frontier. At matched per-GPU throughput, the modeled SubGPU frontier provides up to 2.2x higher per-user throughput than temporal execution, and at matched per-user throughput it provides up to 1.9x higher per-GPU throughput. To test physical feasibility and further validate the simulation results, silicon experiments are performed, using one B200 GPU to emulate a 32-GPU B200 deployment. The experiment evaluates one selected two-stage pipeline configuration at global batch 2,048 using CUDA Green Contexts and TensorRT-LLM kernels. Results show that SubGPU Pipelining improves mean DRAM read-plus-write throughput from 71.8% to 83.6% of peak, and reduces the 36-layer decoder iteration time by 10.33%.

items.title: XBot-Omni: An Omni-Modal Model for Embodied Understanding and Interaction
items.summary: Embodied interaction requires an agent to integrate multimodal perception with verbal and nonverbal behaviors to effectively communicate its intentions, including speech, body motion, and facial expressions. We present XBot-Omni, a Thinker--Talker--Actor architecture that extends the Omni paradigm to robotic modalities, including body motion and facial expressions, with ``X'' representing the extensibility to robotic-specific modalities. The Thinker processes text, images, audio, and video to formulate contextually appropriate responses, which are then realized by the Talker and Actor through speech and coordinated bodily expressions, respectively. In this report, we innovatively introduce the concept of ``Actor'' as a dedicated component for embodied agents: a coordinated, streaming module that leverages the native representations of the Thinker and Talker within an end-to-end pipeline, introducing only modest latency overhead. This unified architecture enables multimodal generation conditioned on omni-modal inputs directly to prevent information loss in staged designs. We comprehensively evaluate XBot-Omni across seven benchmarks, demonstrating strong multimodal understanding capabilities on both general-domain and robot-centric videos, as well as high-quality, natural, and well-coordinated motion generation. Furthermore, our results validate its capability to generate embodied multimodal responses directly from omni inputs, meeting the diverse requirements of embodied interaction. XBot-Omni enables robots not only to perceive the omni world but also to express themselves through speech and bodily behaviors, extending Omni models from conversational interaction to embodied communication in physical environments.

items.title: Accelerating Distributed Variational Quantum Computing over Wireless Networks with Incentive Mechanism Design
items.summary: Distributed variational quantum computing (DVQC) appears as the emerging paradigm to address the limitations of near-term quantum devices by decomposing large parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs) into smaller subcircuits executed across multiple quantum processors. In this context, how to incentivize quantum processors to participate actively is crucial for accelerating DVQC, yet remains largely unexplored in the literature. To address this significant gap, we propose a novel two-stage incentive framework for wireless DVQC. In the first stage, we minimize processor-side energy cost via a joint optimization of subcircuit parameters, number of noise measurements, and transmit power, efficiently solved using block coordinate descent (BCD) and successive convex approximation (SCA). In the second stage, we maximize aggregator-side system utility by selecting an optimal subset of processors based on their optimized energy costs derived from the first stage, formulating a non-convex combinatorial selection problem addressed using the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM). Extensive numerical experiments on the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets demonstrate that our DVQC framework achieves training and testing performance comparable to centralized quantum computing in terms of accuracy and loss, with similar convergence behavior on MNIST and slightly slower initial convergence on CIFAR-10. Moreover, our optimization approach consistently outperforms baseline schemes in energy efficiency and system utility, revealing a strong synergy between processor-level energy minimization and incentive-driven processor selection, where reduced energy costs directly enhances a processor's likelihood of selection and contributes to higher overall system utility.

items.title: Omakase: Execution Congestion Control through Conflict-Graph Integration in Multi-Proposer Blockchain
items.summary: As multi-proposer protocols push consensus throughput, transaction execution has become the dominant bottleneck in blockchains. Layer-1 blockchains parallelize execution either pessimistically (Solana, Sui), requiring upfront state-access declarations and serializing contended transactions, or optimistically (Aptos, Sei, Monad), resolving dependencies at run time but suffering cascading aborts under contention. Both treat blocks in isolation, leaving inter-block parallelism unexploited and most cores idle. We introduce Omakase, a parallel execution framework that combines pre-execution, inter-block conflict-graph integration, and graph-aware Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC). Replicas use idle cores to pre-execute only the blocks they propose, spreading prediction work across concurrent proposers. After building per-block conflict graphs and identifying their hot resources, a greedy scheduler integrates graphs across the blocks committed in a round, keeping an integration only when a lightweight balance heuristic predicts a parallelism gain. A graph-aware OCC executor then runs the integrated graph, admitting transactions in dependency order, which eliminates aborts when the predicted graph is exact and reduces re-executions when it is not. On 15,000 Ethereum mainnet blocks (~2.4M transactions) and synthetic workloads with configurable contention, Omakase reaches a 2.47x speedup over sequential execution, well above single-block OCC and graph-aware baselines. Against the strongest alternative, which runs the whole round as one optimistic window, Omakase matches mean throughput but is markedly more stable under high contention, because integration bounds how much optimistic work is in flight: this is the congestion control of our title. Integration is not free, but overlapping it with execution across rounds hides 94% of its measured cost in the validator pipeline.

items.title: LoCoJAX: Host-Local Coordination for Small-Model RL on TPUs
items.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) increasingly targets small language models, and executing these workloads efficiently across multiple accelerators requires effective coordination. On TPUs, Pathways-based RL uses a single controller to coordinate computation across hosts. This execution model is effective for large models, but its coordination computational costs are harder to amortize when small models repeatedly invoke short computations. To characterize these computational costs, we sweep dense models from 0.6B to 405B parameters on TPU v7x under a decode-heavy workload and measure how host and network computational overhead vary with model size. At 0.6B, host orchestration occupies 36% of step time and network communication 2%, whereas for large models, estimated network computational costs dominate the non-compute time. Motivated by these findings, we present Local Coordination JAX (LoCoJAX), which implements local rollout and reward processing on each TPU host with synchronous global training. In controlled comparisons against a tuned and optimized Pathways baseline on Qwen3-0.6B across three workloads and 8-64 TPU v7x chips, its colocated mode (LoCoJAX-CO) is 1.3-3.6x faster per step; on GSM8K, it completes a step faster on 8 chips than Pathways does on 64. Finally, a Ray-managed disaggregated mode (LoCoJAX-DA) overlaps rollout and training on separate hosts, and placement experiments establish when this overlap compensates for dividing devices and transferring weights: only when rollout dominates the step and receives most of the hosts. On NuminaMath-CoT at 256 chips, giving rollout 75% of hosts cuts step time by about 15% compared with LoCoJAX-CO.

items.title: Fast Serverless LLM Cold Starts by Sharing and Prewarming Startup Work
items.summary: When a serverless LLM platform launches a model worker on demand, the cold start lasts roughly a minute, yet only 5-11% of it is spent loading weights. Most of the remainder goes to compilation, memory profiling and runtime setup, which each server performs again even though the outcome is identical across servers or independent of the model. We present Cairn. The server that is first to start a model publishes the weights and engine artifacts to a CXL memory pool shared across the cluster, and the remaining servers read them in place. Model-independent setup is completed ahead of time inside warm containers, and a template process replaces each container as soon as it is used. With ServerlessLLM on vLLM v0.20, six models from 1B to 14B, and two servers that share an emulated CXL pool, Cairn speeds up cold starts by 4.1-5.2x on servers without a checkpoint of their own and reduces median TTFT on a request stream by 64%.

items.title: NVIDIA Vera: A Microarchitecture-Level Comparison with Grace, Turin, and Granite Rapids
items.summary: The majority of new HPC systems are centered around NVIDIA, AMD, or Intel CPUs. Vera is NVIDIA's latest data-center CPU, including its first custom data-center core design, Olympus. This paper investigates Vera in comparison to AMD Turin and Intel Granite Rapids, using NVIDIA Grace as a baseline. We navigate up the performance ladder, from microbenchmarks that isolate performance metrics, through NAS kernels and miniapps, to single-socket performance of a range of scientific codes. We find that Vera achieves the best performance of the architectures evaluated in most codes tested, and that this gain is primarily attributed to its high memory bandwidth, effective Spatial Multithreading implementation, and low-latency memory subsystem aided by the architecture's predictive structures. While Vera represents a major leap over its predecessor, we show that its comparatively modest floating-point performance trails Intel and AMD in a small number of compute-bound workloads reflecting NVIDIA's GPU focus for such workloads.

items.title: Sub-100KB On-Device CNN Training via Dynamic Sparse Updates and Hardware--Software Co-Design
items.summary: The increasing demand for real-time processing and personalized deep learning has made edge-device training essential but challenging due to high memory and computational costs. To address this, we propose a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) training accelerator with a dynamic sparse update mechanism that selectively updates important parameters using a random channel strategy, avoiding costly evaluations. Combined with activation pruning, our approach reduces activation storage to just 3.4\% of the original. Our hardware features a fused forward dataflow that concurrently processes group normalization and convolution, reducing training time by 45\% through computation reordering and efficient zero-skipping. Implemented in TSMC 28nm at FP8 precision, the design operates at 800 MHz, achieving 8 TOPS peak throughput, 31.13 TOPS/W energy efficiency, and 14.8 TOPS/mm$^2$ area efficiency, with power consumption ranging from 257 to 272 mW. The design enables on-device training within a sub-100KB on-chip SRAM budget (95KB in silicon).

items.title: Fewer Expert Transfers Without Changing Routing: Expert Eviction for MoE Offloading
items.summary: A mixture-of-experts (MoE) language model uses only a few experts per token, so a server can keep most expert weights in CPU memory and copy an expert to the GPU when the router requests it. Recent methods train the router to keep the same experts for several tokens, and treat fewer routing switches as a proxy for fewer copies. We measure the trade-off directly, in a harness that performs and times real CPU-to-GPU copies for OLMoE-1B-7B. On an L40S GPU, every tested policy that holds an expert set fixed and decodes faster than the least-recently-used (LRU) cache increases next-token loss by at least 0.067 nats. A change that leaves every routing decision intact does better: when the cache must evict an expert, evict the one whose next use lies farthest in the future. This rule copies 2.1x fewer experts than LRU at no loss in quality and is within 3.5% of the fewest copies possible. It needs future requests; the next sixteen tokens of demand recover 96% of its reduction, whereas a rule based on counts of past requests recovers 27%.

items.title: CapLite: Prompt-Injection Defense for Small Language Model Agents without Model-Written Security Artifacts
items.summary: Enforcement defenses against prompt injection, such as CaMeL, Progent, IPIGuard and DRIFT, ask the agent's own model to write a security artifact (a program, a privilege policy, a dependency graph or a constraint list) that code then enforces. We ask whether small language model (SLM) agents can be trusted to write these artifacts. Across 15 open-weight models, 13 of them between 1.7B and 12B parameters, they cannot: the policies, graphs and constraints that the agent's model writes admit attacks on 14 (Progent), 13 (IPIGuard) and 11 (DRIFT) of the models, and CaMeL's programs fail to run in up to 68% of episodes. We present CapLite, which derives its policy from the tool schemas, commits the write calls before any tool result is read, and admits a write only if every argument that decides whom or what it affects is stated in the user's request. This guarantees write integrity: injected text cannot add a write, and no write reaches a recipient, amount, object or destination that the user did not state. No attack succeeds in 13,935 attacked AgentDojo episodes. CapLite reaches utility under attack comparable to CaMeL's (29.0% vs. 27.2%) with fewer tokens than every other enforcement defense and than the undefended agent: 17.1k per episode, 18% of CaMeL's, and the highest utility per token of all enforcement defenses.

items.title: Time Flies When You Parallelise: Pareto-efficient Time Series Foundation Models with Linear Recurrences
items.summary: Time series foundation models have demonstrated strong zero-shot forecasting performance, but computational efficiency remains a central architectural challenge. Temporal self-attention incurs quadratic cost in the number of temporal tokens, while nonlinear recurrent state transitions restrict parallel computation along the temporal dimension. We introduce ci-proto, a family of time series foundation models based on Mamba-3, whose linear state recurrences support chunk-wise parallel-in-time computation during training, and inference costs that scale linearly with sequence length. The architecture alternates recurrent temporal processing with cross-variate attention, supporting multivariate probabilistic forecasting with past-only and future-known covariates. Across fev-bench's 100 forecasting tasks, ci-proto XL sets a new state of the art among time series foundation models. The five ci-proto variants also make up the entire Pareto frontier for mean scaled quantile loss and mean absolute scaled error against both parameter count and median runtime.

items.title: UniPipe: Unified Inference Serving and Fine-Tuning for Deadline-Constrained DNN Surrogate Workflows
items.summary: DNN surrogates are increasingly used to accelerate scientific workflows that must process high-rate sensor streams in near real time, exemplified by Ptychographic imaging at next-generation X-ray light sources. Such surrogates deliver 100-1000x higher throughput than iterative solvers, enabling faster steering of experiments. To preserve surrogate accuracy during an experiment, as the input distribution evolves, state-of-the-art deployments freeze the pretrained surrogate or run a separate CUDA context that fine-tunes concurrently with serving. However, multi-context concurrency causes significant contention on the GPU, inflating both the mean and the variance of inference latency, triggering deadline misses in workflows where sensor data has to be processed within a hard per-unit deadline. To address this challenge, we propose UniPipe, a single-context system that unifies inference serving and fine-tuning of a DNN surrogate on a single edge GPU. UniPipe is driven by three key insights: both serving and fine-tuning require a forward pass and can be fused into one; the per-sample latency of modern GPUs is non-linear in batch size; and the workload is repetitive across intervals, enabling offline scheduling. Specifically, UniPipe fuses training and inference data in a single forward pass with a selective backward pass on the training subset, and uses a polynomial-time scheduler that exploits the latency curve to compute the batch composition. We evaluate UniPipe on a real-world Ptychographic reconstruction workflow with sensor rates up to 5000 patterns/sec.; UniPipe lowers reconstruction MSE by up to 30% and inference MSE by up to 50% over a pretrained baseline, and reduces the deadline-miss rate by 13%-22% over a multi-context baseline. UniPipe's unified deployment reduces the latency spread from 106% to 57% of the mean, and increases total throughput compared to multi-context baseline.

items.title: Ropedia Xperience 2: A Gold Standard for Scaling Physical AI Environments and Behaviors
items.summary: Large foundation models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 have recently been shown to control robots directly from visual observations. They nevertheless remain brittle on long-horizon, contact-rich tasks in real-world environments. Further progress depends on two complementary resources: demonstrations of human behavior that supervise how tasks are performed, and interactive environments in which policies can be rolled out, evaluated, and improved in closed loop. Language models have advanced along well-characterized scaling laws; the corresponding question for physical AI is how capability scales with environments and behaviors, which first requires identifying which data to scale and how to produce and reuse such data continuously. To address this question, we introduce Ropedia Xperience 2, comprising 1,589 released metric-scale 3D scans and a collection of 4,230 egocentric recordings of 74 tasks (131 hours). We further show that each capture can be repurposed for robot learning: scenes are converted into physically interactive simulation environments, human motion is retargeted to whole-body robot trajectories, and additional robot behaviors are obtained through virtual teleoperation and automated long-horizon trajectory generation. We propose this joint capture of environments and behaviors as a gold standard for physical AI data collection, laying a data foundation for establishing scaling laws over environments and behaviors.

items.title: Inner Product Regularization for Imitation Learning
items.summary: Robots that learn from demonstrations should extrapolate their policy despite state perturbations such as sensor noise, scene variation, and compounding errors. One approach to this robustness is regularization. Prior regularizers consider each state on its own and limit how sensitive the policy is to any perturbation at that state. By contrast, we explore how the policy's output shifts when given the same perturbation at different states. Our insight is that, locally, the robot should respond to state perturbations in a consistent manner: e.g., if changing an irrelevant object position does not impact the policy at one state, that same change should not shift the policy output at a nearby state. Applying this insight, we develop inner product regularization (InneR). We show that the inner product on action space induces an inner product on state space through the policy Jacobian (the Fisher information for stochastic policies), and that the null space of this inner product governs which state perturbations have a first-order effect on the policy. By clustering states whose inner products are aligned, averaging the inner products within each cluster, and minimizing the smallest eigenvalues of that average, InneR shapes the learned policy so that nearby states share a common null space. InneR enforces consistent responses to perturbations without limiting policy expressiveness, and can be appended to existing imitation learning pipelines for deterministic or stochastic policies. In simulated experiments, InneR makes learned policies more robust to irrelevant state dimensions and shifts between training and test distributions, whereas norm penalties often perform worse than behavior cloning. On a real robot arm performing three manipulation tasks, InneR raises the average success rate of a diffusion policy from 18% to 57% without additional data.

items.title: Sustainable Federated Fine-Tuning with LoRA: Environmental Impact and Performance Footprint
items.summary: Federated Learning (FL) with Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) enables efficient adaptation of Large Language Models (LLMs), yet its energy and carbon costs across hardware remain poorly understood. We evaluated federated Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning on NVIDIA A40, RTX 6000 Ada, and A100 GPUs using a $2^2$ full factorial design with 135M/360M models and 10/100 local steps. CodeCarbon tracked energy and estimated CO$_2$-equivalent emissions. Descriptive allocation of variation assigned 84.8-91.2% of energy and emissions variation to local steps within these ranges. On A40 and RTX 6000 Ada, configurations with fewer steps achieved comparable accuracy with roughly 6-8-fold lower energy consumption and higher accuracy per kWh. items.title: Locality Meets Interference: Structure and Scheduling in Radio Multicasting
items.summary: We study multipoint-to-multipoint multicasting in synchronous radio networks with unknown participant locations and unrestricted message aggregation. Let $n$ be the network size, $k$ the number of participants, and $d$ their hop diameter. A supplied distance-two coloring with $C$ colors yields completion within $(C-1)d+1$ slots and at most $nk$ transmissions. In unit disk graphs, coordinates, one-hop neighbor data, and a common degree bound $Δ_0$ suffice for a $15(Δ_0+1)$-color schedule. A known fixed separation bound permits optimal deterministic $Θ(d)$ completion from coordinates alone. Without geometric data, strong selectivity gives $O(d\min\{n,(Δ_0+1)^2\log n\})$ slots when $n$ is known. Independent random transmission gives $O((Δ_0+1)(d+\log(k/η)))$ slots with failure probability at most $η$; for fixed $Δ_0$, this simplifies to $O(d+\log(1/η))$. A star construction shows that the logarithmic term is necessary for this random rule when the degree grows. We extend color schedules to fixed deletions and subgraphs connected over bounded windows of cycles. Separate conditional reductions preserve additive costs under diameter guessing and control parameter-table and cluster preprocessing. Finally, a counterexample shows that pruning and reranking a breadth-first tree can destroy interference-free delivery. For one-hop designated delivery with receiver degree at most $b$, we prove that the optimal schedule length equals the chromatic number of an associated conflict graph and is at most $2b-1$, with matching examples.

items.title: Autonomous Mobile Robots on a Computing Field
items.summary: We introduce CABOT, a computational model for autonomous mobile robots in which the discrete plane the robots operate on is not a passive stage but an active computing medium. In the classical Look-Compute-Move (LCM) model every increase in computational capability is obtained by strengthening the robots themselves, with lights, memory or wider visibility, at a cost paid once per robot. CABOT strengthens the environment instead: each cell of the grid holds a state from a finite set Q, the states evolve synchronously under a uniform local rule that also senses whether a robot stands on the cell, that is, the floor is a cellular automaton, and the Look operation returns the states of the visible cells in addition to the positions of the visible robots. The robots are as weak as we can make them: oblivious, silent, lightless, myopic with visibility range 1, without multiplicity detection and unable to write to the floor. The number of field states |Q|, rather than any robot capability, becomes the measure of the resources required. On an inert floor (|Q| = 1) such robots can neither form a line, nor gather from scattered positions, nor explore a grid. We show that a handful of states changes this. Line Formation from connected configurations is solvable with four states, and field-silently, so that the floor also reaches a fixed point, with five. Gathering from arbitrary, possibly disconnected, configurations is solvable with three states and Line Formation from arbitrary configurations with six; we prove that neither can be solved field-silently with any number of states. A single robot explores every finite grid forever with four states and every torus with two, which is optimal. Further rule sets, validated by simulation only, equalize the spacing of robots on a row, fill a pattern painted on the floor and guide robots through a maze, and indicate the range of the model.

items.title: SBA: A Practical Memory Performance Denial-of-Service Attack
items.summary: Modern cloud platforms use memory bandwidth regulation to isolate co-located workloads, implicitly assuming that high aggregate bandwidth consumption implies high interference. We show that this assumption is fundamentally flawed. We present the Single-Bank Attack (SBA), a practical memory denial-of-service attack that induces extreme cross-core slowdowns---over three orders of magnitude on memory-intensive victims (e.g., LLM decode)---while consuming less than 1 GB/s of memory bandwidth. SBA exploits the gap between peak and worst-case DRAM throughput by concentrating memory write operations on a single bank, forcing persistent row conflicts and frequent write draining, thereby collapsing the memory service rate. Across Intel and AMD systems, including DDR5- and HBM2E-based platforms, SBA consistently causes orders-of-magnitude slowdowns under realistic multi-tenant settings, revealing a fundamental limitation of bandwidth-centric memory isolation. We further show that this localized contention propagates system-wide: single-bank congestion saturates memory controller queues and induces back-pressure into shared cache and coherence structures, ultimately throttling memory request injection across cores. Consequently, severe interference can arise even at low aggregate bandwidth, evading existing bandwidth-based QoS mechanisms such as Intel RDT MBA. To address this limitation, we propose IQ-MemGuard, a lightweight, software-based memory bandwidth regulator that detects sustained contention using microarchitectural signals and selectively throttles pathological request injection. Our implementation on an Intel platform effectively mitigates SBA, whereas Intel's hardware QoS mechanism fails completely.

items.title: Starscream: Reimagining LLM Sharding on AMD Instinct GPUs with GPU Partitioning
items.summary: As GPU accelerators grow larger to meet rising compute demands, they exhibit increasingly pronounced non-uniform memory access (NUMA) characteristics that challenge existing LLM frameworks. Chiplet-based architectures provide a practical path to larger GPUs while mitigating manufacturing yield constraints. Modern GPUs such as AMD Instinct MI300X employs such a multi-die design, and further offer GPU partitioning capabilities, partitioning a single physical GPU into multiple logical devices with NUMA-aware memory domains, promising faster kernel launches, and reduced memory access latencies with improved locality. However, current parallelization strategies, designed for homogeneous GPU topologies, when applied under partitioning, extend its unidimensional sharding causing significant performance degradation. Three bottlenecks emerge: (1) memory redundancy; (2) arithmetic intensity collapse; (3) communication overhead from flat collectives. We present Starscream, a rethinking of LLM sharding for the chiplet era. Rather than stretching inter-GPU sharding thinner, Starscream adds intra-GPU sharding along an orthogonal dimension, grounded in three foundational principles: kernel shape preservation, memory redundancy elimination, and communication overhead minimization. These principles form the basis for extending any sharding strategy into the partitioning regime. We demonstrate their effectiveness using tensor parallelism as a case study. On AMD MI300X and MI355X, exploiting partitioning capabilities yields up to 4x speedup for attention and 1.43x for fused GEMMs compared to chiplet-oblivious baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of chiplet-aware designs. Starscream's principles generalize across sharding strategies and future architectures.

items.title: UAV-Flow++: A Unified Suite for Benchmarking and Learning Language-Guided UAV Flight
items.summary: Language-guided UAV navigation has largely focused on long-horizon route planning, leaving short-range, object-relative flight maneuvers underexplored. To address this gap, we formulate Flying-on-a-Word (Flow), a task requiring a UAV to convert concise natural-language instruction, egocentric visual observation, and current state dynamics into continuous flight actions. Flow encompasses both primitive motion commands and complex object-interactive behaviors, assessing motion intent comprehension and spatial context grounding. To enable policy learning and closed-loop evaluation, we introduce UAV-Flow, a comprehensive dataset comprising 30,692 expert-piloted real-world trajectories across eight distinct motion categories, alongside 10,109 simulation trajectories in the UAV-Flow-Sim environment equipped with task-specific completion criteria. Furthermore, we develop FlowVLA, which undergoes imitation pretraining on mixed real-sim demonstrations and online post-training via Tail-Aware GRPO (TGRPO). By leveraging group reward distributions, TGRPO effectively reinforces high-reward action sequences. Evaluated on 273 held-out UAV-Flow-Sim episodes, pretrained FlowVLA achieves a mean success rate of 75.58%, outperforming the strongest baseline by 6.72 percentage points, which TGRPO post-training further elevates to 93.16% with superior sample efficiency. Physical UAV experiments demonstrate robust execution of object-relative commands in both indoor and outdoor real-world scenes. Together, Flow establishes a novel benchmark and learning framework for language-conditioned flight maneuvers.
